newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Two kidnapped Russian priests freed in Chechnya.
newsitem.headline: Two kidnapped Russian priests freed in Chechnya.

text.p: Two Russian Orthodox priests kidnapped in Chechnya two weeks ago were released unharmed on Friday just three days before the breakaway region goes to the polls.

Father Yevfimy and his assistant Alexei told reporters in the capital Grozny that they had not been ill-treated. He said they had little idea where they had been, who had seized them or why they were finally handed over.

Interior ministry officials of Chechnya's secessionist administration, though clearly relieved the incident had ended peacefully, were also unforthcoming. They said only that "steps were taken" by the ministry to secure the priests' release.
One senior official insisted, however, that the kidnapping had been the work of "criminals" and had no political motive.
Dark-bearded Yevfimy, looking tired and thin but otherwise in good health, said their captors told them they wanted to exchange the priests for "someone who was in jail".

The kidnapping, coming after the killing of six foreign Red Cross workers and the death of several ethnic Russians, heightened tension in the mainly Moslem region on the eve of presidential and parliamentary elections.

Father Yevfimy was driving in the countryside on January 9 on a mission to locate the grave of his predecessor at the main Russian Orthodox church in Grozny. That priest went missing a year ago and was recently reported murdered.
Yevfimy and Alexei were seized from their car and kept locked away for two weeks, surviving mostly on a diet of bread.

"We just sat and waited patiently and prayed," Yevfiny said, adding that he feared his experience would scare off Russian priests from coming to Chechnya to serve the region's dwindling ethnic Russian community.
"But I hope that after the elections, the post of president will be occupied by an honourable man who can establish order and allow people in Chechnya to live in peace," he said.
The front-runners in Monday's presidential vote are all leading figures in the guerrilla movement that forced Moscow to withdraw its troops last year after 21 month of war.
All of them have pledged to turn Chechnya's de facto autonomy into independence.
Moscow agreed to the elections but has since criticised them.
